analysis.one_liner: Lets the U.S. sue foreign oil cartels for fixing prices and creates a Justice Department task force on oil markets.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 324-84 with heavy bipartisan support on May 20, 2008, but the Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal under U.S. antitrust law for foreign oil cartels like OPEC to limit production or set prices that affect the American market, would strip those states of their legal immunity from such suits, and would let the Attorney General sue them in federal court. It would also create a Justice Department task force to investigate gasoline price gouging, refinery supply manipulation, and oil futures trading, and order a government study of whether past oil merger settlements protected competition. [S2, S3, S4]
analysis.who_benefits: American drivers and gasoline buyers. In May 2008 gasoline was near $4 a gallon, and the bill targeted foreign state cartels that restrict oil output, while directing a new Justice Department task force to examine gouging, withheld refinery capacity, and futures-market manipulation that raise pump prices. [S2, S3, S4]

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Sherman Act to make it illegal for foreign states or their agents to limit oil production, fix prices, or restrain trade when the effects reach the U.S. market. [S2, S4]

Denies foreign states engaged in such conduct sovereign immunity, so U.S. courts can hear enforcement cases against them, and bars courts from using the act-of-state doctrine to avoid ruling on the merits. [S2, S4]
Authorizes the Attorney General to sue in U.S. district court to enforce the ban. [S2, S4]

Creates a Department of Justice Petroleum Industry Antitrust Task Force required to examine gasoline price gouging, collusion restricting refinery capacity, price discrimination against retailers, supply withholding to inflate prices, and manipulation of oil futures markets, and to report to Congress annually. [S3, S4]

Orders a Government Accountability Office study of whether the divestitures required in past petroleum merger consent decrees actually preserved competition, with findings referred to the task force for possible enforcement action. [S3, S4]

analysis.who_pays: OPEC member states and their national oil companies, which could face antitrust suits for production limits, and U.S. oil companies, which face new Justice Department scrutiny of gouging, refinery capacity, and trading practices. A further risk falls on consumers if oil-producing countries retaliate by cutting output or a lawsuit escalates into a supply or diplomatic conflict.
analysis.who_pays_short: Foreign oil cartels and major oil companies

drawbacks.text: Suing OPEC governments over production quotas, which are sovereign policy decisions, is legally and diplomatically untested; oil-producing states could retaliate by trimming output or cooling cooperation with Washington, which could raise prices rather than lower them. [S2, S4]

The bill's domestic pieces depend on the Attorney General's discretion: the task force must study and report but is not required to bring any enforcement action, so consumers get no guaranteed relief even if it became law. [S3, S4]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside for consumers is real but uncertain: the Sherman Act was written for private conspirators, and forcing it onto foreign governments' production policy may accomplish little in court, while provoking retaliation is the serious cost an honest supporter had to weigh. The task force and the merger study are modest, low-cost steps that could improve enforcement against refiners and traders, but they are information-gathering, not relief at the pump.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 324-84, the Senate placed it on its calendar, and it died there without a vote when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Introduced May 15, 2008 by Rep. Steve Kagen (D-WI) with 19 Democratic cosponsors, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee. [S1, S5, S6]
The House bypassed committee action and brought the bill straight to the floor the next legislative day under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure, which requires a two-thirds majority. [S6]
On May 20, 2008 the House passed it 324-84: 221 of 235 Democrats voted yes (2 no) and 103 of 199 Republicans voted yes (82 no). [S7]
The Senate received the bill on May 21, 2008, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 744, where no further action occurred. [S4, S6]
The bill never received a Senate vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009. [S1, S6]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Foreign oil-producing states kept limiting output with no exposure to U.S. antitrust suits, and major oil companies avoided the new Justice Department task force scrutiny of gouging, refinery capacity, and futures trading that the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign oil states and major oil companies

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill, bringing it to the floor.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor after it was placed on the calendar, letting it die without a vote.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration opposed NOPEC legislation, saying suing OPEC would backfire, and had threatened a veto of a similar bill the previous year.

against.name: 82 of 199 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on the motion to suspend the rules and pass the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats backed it nearly unanimously, 221-2, while Republicans split 103 for and 82 against. [S7]

industries.industry: OPEC member states and their national oil companies
industries.note: The bill strips their sovereign immunity and exposes their production limits and price coordination to antitrust suits by the Justice Department. Their output restrictions are what pushed U.S. gasoline prices up, so their interest runs directly against drivers. [S2, S4]

industries.industry: Major integrated oil companies and refiners
industries.note: The task force must examine gouging, collusion restricting refinery capacity, supply withholding, and price discrimination against retailers, opening them to possible enforcement, though the bill mandates studies and reports rather than action. Their interest in keeping that scrutiny dormant runs against consumers. [S3, S4]

The task force is directed to examine anticompetitive manipulation in petroleum futures markets, adding scrutiny to trading practices, but with no required enforcement. Manipulation in these markets feeds directly into what drivers pay. [S4]
